final: Overall, the Seed Secondary Schools hold the majority of assets 63.4% (145,256), followed by Health Centres with 27.7% (63,432). final: Verification also noted that 13,520 assets, mainly in seed secondary schools and Health Centres, were classified as faulty and out of use. Notable among the facilities include Lungulu Seed Secondary School in Nwoya District where desktop computers, a printer and UPS units were still boxed because the school was waiting for power connection. final: The exercise recorded 16,663 assets of the different categories across all the thirteen asset-holding Ministries and agencies. In terms of categorization, the exercise recorded 15,192 ICT equipment items including desktop computers, laptops, tablets and Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) units, 77 transport items, 99 furniture and fittings, 48 other classified assets, 1,235 items outside fixed-asset classification and 12 unclassified entries.

final: At MDA level, apart from sixteen faulty assets at Ministry of Works and Transport, one faulty double-cabin pickup at Ministry of Health and three faulty laptops at the Office of the Prime minister, the rest of the assets, 16,643 (99.9%), were recorded as functional and in use. LGFC and MoPS indicated that they never received UgIFT assets.

body_blocks.text: The findings show a substantial stock of UgIFT assets supporting health care and secondary education, alongside equipment and buildings requiring attention. Facilities reported improvements in their services, but unfinished works, equipment out of use and weaknesses in asset identification limit the benefits. The report sets out the action needed to maintain the assets, complete outstanding works and resolve errors in the financial and custody records.

body_blocks.text: A total of 229,024 asset records were identified. Schools account for 145,256 and Health Centres for 63,432. A further 16,663 relate to ministries and agencies, 602 to regional blood banks, 3,067 to hospitals under local governments and four to other local-government locations. The total includes items whose receipt, classification or programme assignment still requires confirmation. These cases must be resolved before the full population can be certified as physically verified UgIFT assets.

body_blocks.text: Overall, 215,504 items (94.1%) are classified Functional and 13,520 (5.9%) Faulty, with the same numbers recorded as in use and out of use, respectively. Reasons for non-use include lack of power, unfinished buildings, missing parts and insufficient training. These require different responses. Usable tag details are unavailable for 178,695 items, making identification and custody checks a substantial task.

body_blocks.text: Facilities reported improvements in services following UgIFT support. Of 284 health-centre respondents, 238 (83.8%) reported at least one benefit, including improved maternity services, access to care and use of equipment. Of 193 school respondents, 144 (74.6%) reported benefits such as better learning conditions and access to secondary education. These are the facilities’ accounts of changes in their services; the exercise did not measure how much of each change was caused by the programme.

body_blocks.text: This report presents the findings of the UgIFT asset verification undertaken by the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development as part of programme closure activities. It sets out the status of the assets provided by the programme to the targeted national institutions responsible for supporting the implementation of the programme, Blood Banks and local governments specifically targeting Seed Secondary Schools and health facilities upgraded from Health Centre II to Health Centre III.

body_blocks.text: The Uganda Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers (UgIFT) Programme is a government programme implemented through a Programme-for-Results (PforR) launched and aligned with the broader IGFT Reform Programme (2015). UgIFT 1.0 began with US$200 million in FY2017/18, supporting Education and Health. This was later expanded through additional financing of US$300 million, including US$240 million in credit and US$60 million in grants, with US$50 million from the IDA Refugee Support Window, expanding beyond Education and Health to water and Environment and Agriculture (micro-scale irrigation) making the overall funding total of US$500 million.
body_blocks.accepted: The Uganda Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers (UgIFT) Programme is a government programme implemented through a Programme-for-Results (PforR) launched and aligned with the broader IGFT Reform Programme (2015). UgIFT 1.0 began with US$200 million in FY2017/18, supporting Education and Health. This was later expanded through additional financing of US$300 million, including US$240 million in credit and US$60 million in grants, with US$50 million from the IDA Refugee Support Window, expanding beyond Education and Health to water and Environment and Agriculture (micro-scale irrigation) making the overall funding total of US$500 million.

body_blocks.text: The Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfer Reform Programme (IGFT RP) was revised in 2020 to align with the Third National Development Plan (NDP III 2020/21 - 2024/25), and to directly contribute to Four (04) Programmes i.e. Human Capital Development; Public Sector Transformation; Natural Resources, Environment, Climate change, Land and Water Management; and Development Plan Implementation.

body_blocks.text: Overall, the development objective of the UgIFT Programme was to: “Improve the adequacy, equity, and effectiveness of financing and the oversight, management, and delivery of Local Government services in Education, Health, Water and Environment, and Agriculture (micro-scale irrigation), including refugees and their host communities”.

body_blocks.text: 2.8 Challenges and Limitations to the assignment
body_blocks.accepted: 2.8 Challenges and Limitations to the assignment

body_blocks.text: Difficult terrain and poor physical accessibility of facilities: Physical accessibility presented a significant operational challenge especially for facilities located in areas characterised by difficult terrain and limited transport accessibility such as Bwesumbu HC III, Bwesumbu Seed School, Buhuhira and Kabingo in Kasese District. In addition, accessing facilities within the Island was difficult, time consuming and expensive. This led the teams to overshoot the anticipated time for data collection.
body_blocks.accepted: Difficult terrain and poor physical accessibility of facilities: Physical accessibility presented a significant operational challenge especially for facilities located in areas characterised by difficult terrain and limited transport accessibility such as Bwesumbu HC III, Bwesumbu Seed School, Buhuhira and Kabingo in Kasese District. In addition, accessing facilities within the Island was difficult, time consuming and expensive. This led the teams to overshoot the anticipated time for data collection.

body_blocks.text: High transportation cost: Given the national wide coverage, the rising fuel prices led to high field costs. The field teams spent more money than was anticipated. The costs were extra ordinarily higher for island facilities like Kalangala, Buvuma, Mayuge among others. For instance, Kalangala had 3 facilities with long distance on water that required hiring a private boat since it was not a common route to the transporters and outside the ferry schedules. A similar situation was encountered in Buvuma and Namayingo districts.

body_blocks.text: Poor record keeping: In many LGs and facilities, there were no clear records about the assets delivered under UgIFT. The LGs and the facilities had incomplete or missing UgIFT asset registers which delayed data collection. Subsequently, the teams took longer in such facilities identifying the assets as most of these were not engraved with the UgIFT identifiers while others were not engraved at all. In addition, the field teams encountered situations where some Assets could not be physically accessed especially for schools since it was holiday time.

body_blocks.text: The programme list at the LG level contained 629 UgIFT facilities, of which 371 were Health Centres and 258 were Seed Secondary Schools. A further 3,067 assets were attributed to hospitals and four to other local-government locations. The details are presented in sections 3.6 (Health Centres) and 3.7 (Seed Secondary Schools).

body_blocks.text: 4.1 Maintenance and repairs
body_blocks.accepted: 4.1 Maintenance and repairs

body_blocks.text: Maintenance keeps UgIFT assets working for the services they were bought to support. Most of the verified assets are furniture, clinical equipment and computers in daily use at Health Centres and seed schools, where wear and breakage are to be expected. Routine checks, a record of faults and a dependable route for repair decide whether a broken item returns to use quickly or stays out of service. During the verification, each facility was asked how it maintains, repairs, services or replaces UgIFT assets and whether it keeps a regular record of their functionality or breakdown.

body_blocks.text: Frequency. Few facilities worked to a fixed maintenance interval. Of the 494 programme-list facilities that described how they maintain UgIFT assets or check their condition, 50 (10.1%) did so at a fixed interval. Of these 50, 14 (28.0%) worked annually, 11 (22.0%) monthly, 10 (20.0%) quarterly, 9 (18.0%) every school term, 3 (6.0%) twice a year and 3 (6.0%) weekly or daily, as Figure 47 shows. A further 18 facilities (3.6%) described routine or scheduled servicing without a set interval, mostly scheduled visits by regional referral hospital maintenance teams, and 61 (12.3%) repaired items as the need arose. Ngwedo Seed Secondary School in Buliisa engaged a caretaker every month and used the Directorate of Industrial Training for furniture repairs, while Busaale reviewed asset condition every quarter.

body_blocks.text: 5 Recommendations
body_blocks.accepted: 5 Recommendations

body_blocks.text: Recommendation. Facility managers and school governing bodies should keep the local and regional repair arrangements that already work and adopt a fixed routine: a condition check at least every school term in schools and every quarter in health centres, and a full count of UgIFT assets each year. Each facility should keep a condition book or fault list naming each item requiring action, the responsible person and the agreed completion date; the 36 facilities with no repair arrangement and the 80 with no functionality or breakdown record should set these up first.
body_blocks.accepted: Recommendation. Facility managers and school governing bodies should keep the local and regional repair arrangements that already work and adopt a fixed routine: a condition check at least every school term in schools and every quarter in health centres, and a full count of UgIFT assets each year. Each facility should keep a condition book or fault list naming each item requiring action, the responsible person and the agreed completion date; the 36 facilities with no repair arrangement and the 80 with no functionality or breakdown record should set these up first.

body_blocks.text: District health and education offices should review unresolved repairs each quarter and arrange technical assistance, and regional referral hospital workshops should include UgIFT equipment in their scheduled visits. Annual maintenance plans should separate minor repairs from major repairs such that the minor repairs be met from Primary Health Care funds or school grants, while major repairs can be handled through district or national funding.

Annual maintenance plans should separate minor repairs from major repairs such that the minor repairs be met from Primary Health Care funds or school grants, while major repairs can be handled through district or national funding.

body_blocks.text: Recommendation. Facility managers, district health and education officers, engineers and technical teams should prioritise unsafe furniture, electrical concerns and failed equipment needed for essential services. Withdraw unsafe items, obtain technical assessments and verify safe operation after repair. The broken down and not functional assets should be assessed in order of their effect on care and teaching, beginning with clinical equipment and the school furniture that makes up most of the broken down assets; items beyond economic repair should receive a formal disposal decision. At national level, the Office of the Prime Minister should decide on repair or replacement of its three laptops recorded as faulty, and Uganda Blood Transfusion Services (UBTS) should repair or replace the six blood-pressure machines recorded as faulty at Arua Regional Blood Bank. Keep damaged assets separate from usable assets awaiting installation so that each receives the appropriate action.

body_blocks.text: Recommendation. LG Accounting Officers, engineers, health and education officers and contractors should coordinate outstanding buildings, utilities, furniture and equipment through site-specific completion plans for each of the 83 documented facilities with works or handover outstanding, comprising seventy with incomplete works and thirteen awaiting handover or commissioning. These are documented minimums. Installation should follow confirmation that rooms, power, water and security are ready. Stored assets described as new or in good condition should be issued to the rooms where they are needed, and each asset waiting for power or installation should have a named date for connection and testing. Protect services already operating during construction. There should be complete testing and signing off before handover or closing each action.

body_blocks.text: Recommendation. District health officers, facility managers, suppliers and regional technical teams should provide practical training for staff who use specialist equipment, starting with the Health Centres that linked idle equipment to a lack of skills, including oxygen equipment users, for example, at Bubago and Sop Sop and staff requiring orientation at Avogera. Handover should include a demonstration, basic maintenance guidance and a named route for technical support. Future supply contracts should make on-site demonstration to the staff who will use the equipment, a condition of acceptance and staffing reviews should take account of the equipment each health centre now holds.
